lab.summary: Three small programs, three deliberate sins — the leak, the double-free, the realloc move. Commit each one, watch the consequence with your own eyes, then fix it and state the fix as a one-sentence ownership rule. Compile everything with `cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra`.

steps.title: Sin 1 — commit the leak
steps.detail: Write the leak program: a loop of 5 rounds × 10 allocations, each `malloc(10 << 20)` (10 MiB) deliberately never freed, with `memset(p, 1, 10 << 20)` touching every page so the memory is real — without touching the pages the OS hands out virtual address space lazily and the climb is nearly invisible (the first version of this demo without `memset` showed ~2 MB per round; a leak you can't observe is still a leak). A `peak_rss_kb()` helper using `getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF, …)` reports the process's peak resident memory after each round. Compile and run.

steps.title: Sin 1 — observe the RSS climb
steps.detail:
Observed output on the author's machine:

```text
start: peak RSS 1344 KB
after 100 MiB: peak RSS 103936 KB
after 200 MiB: peak RSS 206496 KB
after 300 MiB: peak RSS 309056 KB
after 400 MiB: peak RSS 411616 KB
after 500 MiB: peak RSS 514176 KB
```

Memory climbs almost exactly 100 MB per round — every leaked byte accounted for. Note the exit: the program ends and the OS reclaims all 500 MB instantly. A leak only matters *during* the process's lifetime — which is why a leak in a short-lived demo is invisible and a leak in a long-running daemon or a 20-year PLC is a reliability bug.

steps.title: Sin 1 — fix it and state the rule
steps.detail:
**Fix:** free each block before losing the pointer (move `free(p)` inside the loop, after `memset`). Rebuild, rerun, watch RSS stay flat.

**State the rule:** *every allocation is freed exactly once on every path, before its last handle is lost.*

steps.title: Sin 2 — commit the double-free
Sin 2 — observe the allocator's kill
steps.detail:
Observed behaviour on the author's machine:

```text
allocated 0x103651990
freed once — fine
Trace/BPT trap: 5            ← the process is killed; exit status 133
```

The allocator detected the second `free` of a live-once block and killed the process on the spot — the third `printf` never ran. Honesty about your machine: on this macOS (Apple clang, arm64) the abort arrives as `SIGTRAP` with no diagnostic printed to stderr (the detailed message goes to the system log); on glibc/Linux the same sin typically prints `double free or corruption (!prev)` and dies with `SIGABRT`. Different allocators, different last words, same cause of death.

steps.title: Sin 2 — fix it and state the rule
steps.detail:
**Fix:** delete the second `free`. Then adopt the defensive habit: after freeing, set the pointer to `NULL` — `free(NULL)` is a guaranteed no-op, so a repeated free becomes harmless instead of fatal.

**State the rule:** *a block's owner frees it exactly once, and afterwards every pointer to it is dead (set yours to NULL).*

steps.title: Sin 3 — commit the realloc move
steps.detail: Write the realloc program: `malloc` 8 bytes, `strcpy` `"abc"` in, then grow in doublings for 24 iterations with the two-step pattern (`char *t = realloc(p, newcap); if (t == NULL) { free(p); return 1; } p = t;`), printing `cap`, the address, and the contents after each doubling. Compile and run. **Watch the address column.**

steps.title: Sin 3 — observe the moves
steps.detail:
Observed output (the jumps that matter):

```text
cap   8: 0x1040599d0  "abc"
cap  16: 0x1040599d0  "abc"  <- contents preserved across growth
cap  32: 0x1040599e0  "abc"
cap  64: 0x104059a00  "abc"
...
cap 16384: 0xb17004000  "abc"
...
cap 4194304: 0x650000000  "abc"
```

The block moved almost every doubling — sometimes a few bytes up the heap, twice to entirely different regions — and the contents survived every move; `realloc` copied them, that is its job. Now the pointed question: if another pointer — a `char *cursor` walking the string, or a struct field holding `p` — had been stashed anywhere before the move, it would still hold the *old* address, which now belongs to the allocator or to someone else's allocation. This is how the cold open's use-after-free arises in real code: not from a stray `free`, but from a growth operation that invalidated pointers nobody remembered.

steps.title: Sin 3 — fix it and state the rule
steps.detail:
**Fix:** the two-step pattern you see in the listing (never `p = realloc(p, n)`), plus the discipline: after a successful `realloc`, *recompute* every derived pointer from the new base; never cache pointers into a growable buffer across a push.

**State the rule:** *only `realloc`'s return value names the block after a resize — every pointer into the old location is dead the moment the call succeeds.*

lab.closingPrompt: State the three ownership rules from memory: every allocation is freed exactly once on every path, before its last handle is lost · a block's owner frees it exactly once, and afterwards every pointer to it is dead (set yours to `NULL`) · only `realloc`'s return value names the block after a resize — every pointer into the old location is dead the moment the call succeeds. Plus the standing rule: check every allocation for `NULL`.

buildTask.title: The I.4 growable buffer — the Vec ancestor

rubric.criterion: Geometric growth — `cap` doubles; output shows 0 → initial → ×2 → ×4 … and `len` catching up (zero marks: growth is one-per-push or invisible in output)
Free discipline — every allocation freed exactly once, failure path included; double-`buf_free` safe (zero marks: leak, double-free, or crash on any path)
Ownership contract — all three clauses present and *accurate* in `buf.h` comments (zero marks: contract missing, or describes code you didn't write)
`realloc` failure path — `buf_push` returns -1, old buffer intact and usable, two-step pattern used (zero marks: `p = realloc(p, …)` anywhere, or failure corrupts the buffer)
Bounds-checked `buf_get` — out-of-range call returns -1, `*out` untouched, and the demo shows the failure handled (zero marks: reads past `len` return silent garbage, or the check is absent)

stretch: Failure injection: add a compile-time test hook (e.g. `-DFAIL_REALLOC_AT=3`) that makes the *n*-th `realloc` in your demo return `NULL`, and prove in the output that the buffer survives — push fails, old elements still readable, `buf_free` still clean.

Generalize the element type: replace `int` with a `typedef int buf_elem;` in one place, then flip it to `double` and confirm nothing else in the implementation had to change. (The fully generic `void *` version needs material from I.6 — note it, don't build it.)
